questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (1).
questions.solution: 'Not entirely ___' — the comparison to smoking is called mostly but not wholly justified: **fair**. Rare, late and loud have no bearing on whether a comparison is justified.
questions.passage: Doctors now describe sitting as the new smoking, and the comparison is not entirely (1) ___. Hours of uninterrupted sitting slow the circulation, dull the muscles and confuse the metabolism that movement keeps sharp. The trouble is that modern work is built around the chair: screens, meetings and commutes all (2) ___ stillness. Exercise routines sold as the cure assume a willpower that most tired people cannot (3) ___. A simpler prescription is emerging from research: break up the sitting. Standing for two minutes every half hour, walking during phone calls, taking stairs instead of lifts — these small acts do not (4) ___ gym membership, but studies credit them with real gains in energy, mood and blood sugar. The body, it seems, is less impressed by the (5) ___ of occasional heroic workouts than by the rhythm of frequent light movement.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (2).
questions.solution: Work 'is built around the chair', so screens, meetings and commutes all **demand** stillness. Disturb and deny reverse the logic; double is ungrammatical here ('double stillness' adds nothing the frame supports).

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (3).
questions.solution: To call up willpower from within is to **summon** it — the collocation 'summon the willpower' fits 'cannot summon'. The other three verbs do not collocate with willpower.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (4).
questions.solution: Small acts 'do not ___ gym membership' — they **require** no membership. Admire, expire and enquire are sound-alike decoys from the -quire family.
questions.shortcut: -quire trap set: pick by meaning, not by sound.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (5).
questions.solution: The sentence contrasts 'the ___ of occasional heroic workouts' with 'the rhythm of frequent light movement' — showiness vs regularity: **drama**. Drumbeat would support rhythm rather than contrast with it; drowsiness and drainage do not describe workouts' appeal.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

OBLIGATORY
questions.solution: Obligatory = required, **compulsory**. Optional and voluntary are antonyms; doubtful is unrelated.
questions.shortcut: obligation → something forced → compulsory.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

TRANSPARENT
questions.solution: Transparent lets light through; **opaque** blocks it — the standard antonym pair. Clear is a synonym; brightness and fragility are unrelated properties.
questions.shortcut: trans- (through) vs op- (blocking): transparent–opaque.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To bite the dust
questions.solution: Fallen warriors bite the dust — **to fail or be defeated**. The literal dust options are photographable decoys.
questions.shortcut: Falling face-down = losing.

questions.q: Select the correctly spelt word.
questions.solution: Vaccinate has **double c**: vac-cinate (from 'vaccine'). Vacinate drops a c; the other two also distort the ending.
questions.shortcut: vaccine → vaccinate: keep the cc.

questions.q: Select the correctly spelt word.
questions.solution: The spelling is **lieutenant**: l-i-e-u-t-e-n-a-n-t. The pronunciation ('lef-') is a spoken quirk; the letters never change.
questions.shortcut: Write it as lieu + tenant — 'place-holder', its old meaning.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate one word for the given expression.

One who writes the life history of another person
questions.solution: **Biographer** writes another's life; an autobiographer writes his own; a bibliographer lists books; a cartographer draws maps.
questions.shortcut: bio (life) + grapher (writer); auto = self.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

He was accused ___ theft by his employer.
questions.solution: 'Accused **of**' is the fixed collocation: accused of theft, murder, cheating. The other prepositions do not collocate with accuse.
questions.shortcut: accuse of, charge with, suspect of.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The soldiers marched ___ enemy territory at dawn.
questions.solution: Movement to the inside of an area takes **into**: marched into territory. 'In' marks position, not movement; 'at' gives a point; 'onto' needs a surface.
questions.shortcut: movement + area = into.

questions.q:
Select the part of the sentence that has an error.

One should do (a) his duty (b) sincerely (c) No error (d)
questions.solution: 'One' must be followed by **one's**, never his/her/their, when no person is specified: 'One should do one's duty sincerely.'
questions.shortcut: one ... one's — the chain never breaks.

questions.q:
Select the part of the sentence that has an error.

The flowers (a) smells sweet (b) in the garden at dawn (c) No error (d)
questions.solution: Plural subject 'flowers' needs the plural verb **smell**: 'The flowers smell sweet.' (Smell here is a linking verb taking an adjective.)
questions.shortcut: SVA sweep: flowers plural → smell.

questions.q:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the sentence.

This design is more unique than that one.
options: This design is very more unique
questions.solution: 'Unique' means one of a kind — a quality that cannot be graded, so no comparative or superlative is possible: 'This design is unique.'
questions.shortcut: Absolutes (unique, perfect, complete) reject more/most.

questions.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

They will have finished the work by Friday.
options: The work will have been finished by them by Friday.
The work will have finished by them by Friday.
The work will been finished by them by Friday.
The work would have been finished by them by Friday.
questions.solution: Future perfect → **will have been + V3**: 'The work will have been finished by them.' B drops 'been' after will have; C drops 'have'; D shifts the modal to would.
questions.shortcut: will have + V3 → will have been + V3.

questions.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.

A letter is being written by Ravi.
questions.solution: 'Is being + V3' is the present continuous passive → active **is + V-ing**: 'Ravi is writing a letter.' B drops the continuous; C and D change the tense.
questions.shortcut: is being + V3 → is + V-ing.

questions.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

He said, "The sun rises in the east."
options: He said that the sun is rising in the east.
He said that the sun rises in the east.
He said that the sun rose in the east.
He said that the sun had risen in the east.
questions.solution: A universal truth **keeps its tense** even after a past reporting verb: 'The sun rises in the east.' B and C wrongly backshift; D breaks the habitual present.
questions.shortcut: Truth test: facts of nature freeze.

questions.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Teamwork begins with trust. **P:** Members who trust one another share information freely. **Q:** Information sharing prevents costly duplication of work. **R:** Duplicated work, after all, wastes both time and money. **S:** Trust, once broken, is hard to rebuild. **6.** Hence, protect trust above every other resource.
questions.solution: **P** develops S1 (trust → sharing) → **Q** (sharing → no duplication) → **R** (why duplication matters) → **S** (the warning about broken trust) just before S6's 'Hence'. PQRS.
questions.shortcut: Chain the referents: information → duplication → waste; S's warning precedes Hence.

questions.q: What is the central idea of the passage?
options: Transport designed around the single male commute fails women, though practical fixes are cheap and known.
Women should avoid public transport in the evening.
Flyovers are the best use of transport budgets.
Trip chaining is a pattern found only among mothers.
questions.solution: The passage diagnoses male-default design, shows the trip-chaining mismatch, then argues the fixes are simple and cheap. B contradicts the passage's aim; C reverses the budget point; D overstates — the passage uses a mother as an example, not a rule.
questions.shortcut: Thesis = problem + fix: 'designed out' + 'cheaper than flyovers'.
questions.passage:
When city buses and metro coaches are designed for the average male commuter, half the population is quietly designed out. Women's journeys differ from men's in a pattern transport planners call 'trip chaining': a mother may travel from home to a school, from the school to a workplace, and from the workplace to a market before returning home — three short linked trips where a man makes one direct one. Fare systems that charge per boarding punish exactly this pattern, and buses that run every forty minutes turn a chain of errands into a day's work.

Evidence from several cities shows what happens when services are rethought. Where frequencies improved and fares were made transfer-friendly, women's ridership rose sharply; where stations were lit and staffed, women reported feeling safer travelling after dark, and employment among them measurably increased. Safety, it turns out, is not a separate department from economics: a woman who avoids an evening shift to dodge an unsafe platform is a worker the labour market loses.

None of this requires exotic technology. It requires counting women's trips, pricing transfers sensibly, lighting stations and employing staff — most of it cheaper than the flyovers that dominate transport budgets. What stands in the way is imagination: planners still picture a single commuter moving between home and office at fixed hours. The city that plans for the chained trip instead will find it has planned for children, for the elderly, for anyone whose day is a chain rather than a line.

questions.q: In the passage, 'trip chaining' refers to —
options: a direct journey between home and office
several short linked journeys made in a single day
tying luggage to the roof of a bus
a fare system based on the number of boardings
questions.solution: The passage defines it through the mother's example: home → school → workplace → market, 'three short linked trips'. C describes per-boarding fares, the thing that *punishes* chaining; D is the male-pattern journey the passage contrasts it with.
questions.shortcut: Defined-in-place terms: the dash after the colon carries the definition.

questions.q: According to the passage, where stations were lit and staffed, —
options: women felt safer after dark and their employment increased
questions.solution: The evidence sentence: women 'reported feeling safer travelling after dark, and employment among them measurably increased.' B, C and D are not linked to lighting and staffing anywhere in the passage.
questions.shortcut: Detail = locate the 'where stations were lit' clause and read forward.

questions.q: It can be inferred that per-boarding fare systems are criticised in the passage because they —
options: are too expensive for single direct trips
cannot be used on metro coaches
were designed for children and the elderly
penalise journeys that involve several stops
questions.solution: Charging per boarding punishes the multi-stop chained trip that women typically make — that is the explicit logic ('punish exactly this pattern'). A single direct trip pays once and is unaffected, so B fails; C and D invert the design history.
questions.shortcut: Pronoun 'this pattern' points back at trip chaining — the answer sits there.

questions.q: The expression 'exotic technology' as used in the passage suggests something —
questions.solution: 'None of this requires exotic technology' means the needed fixes are ordinary and simple — 'exotic' here = **unusual and elaborate**, not imported. The contrast with 'cheaper than the flyovers' confirms the sense of elaborate expense.
questions.shortcut: Context defines the word: fixes are plain, so exotic = fancy.
